analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to competitive oil and gas leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after its January 1991 referral, the Senate Energy Committee took no action, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Mineral Leasing Act of 1920 to direct the Interior Department to sell oil and gas leases on the public lands of Alaska's Arctic coastal plain — the 1.5-million-acre area set aside by Congress in 1980 for study, known today as part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. It required a first lease sale within twelve months of passage, declared a 1987 federal study sufficient to satisfy all environmental review requirements for leasing, and directed the Secretary to provide aid to North Slope communities affected by development [S2] [S3]. Supporters argued the area held 4.8 to 29.4 billion barrels of oil and would reduce dependence on foreign oil [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain the right to bid on and develop leases across the coastal plain, with leases up to 2,560 acres each and initial terms of up to ten years [S3]. The state of Alaska and North Slope communities would gain federal impact aid, planning assistance, and a share of bonus bids and royalties [S3]. Consumers and national security were the stated beneficiaries, through more domestic oil production [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies and Alaska's state government

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Secretary to establish and promptly implement a competitive oil and gas leasing program to assure expeditious exploration, development, and production on the Coastal Plain, with the first lease sale within twelve months of enactment [S2] [S3].

Cites federal estimates that the coastal plain holds 4.8 to 29.4 billion barrels of crude oil in place, and argues new North Slope production would reduce dependence on foreign oil, lower fuel costs for consumers, create jobs, and add bonus bid and royalty revenue to the Treasury [S3].
Directs the Secretary to provide impact aid and planning help to North Slope communities so public services could absorb the effects of development [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental cost: permanent industrial development of the coastal plain of what is now the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, with risk to the Porcupine caribou herd, migratory birds, and the Gwich'in and Inupiat communities that rely on the area. The bill's protections are discretionary — the Secretary must only ensure 'reasonable protection' of wildlife, the environment, and subsistence users — and it bars any new environmental studies by declaring the 1987 Coastal Plain Resource Assessment sufficient to meet all legal review requirements [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill declares the 1987 Coastal Plain Resource Assessment and its environmental impact statement sufficient to satisfy all requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act for leasing decisions, and states that 'no further studies, reports, or assessments shall be required' — meaning leasing would proceed on 25-year-old analysis with no updated review of wildlife or subsistence impacts [S3].

Environmental protections rest on a 'reasonable protection' standard left to the Secretary's discretion, with mitigation conditions only for effects the Secretary deems 'reasonably foreseeable' — the same standard's adequacy was the central dispute in the decades-long ANWR fight [S3].

Once leases are issued for up to ten years and extended as long as oil is produced, development of the coastal plain would be effectively irreversible, foreclosing wilderness protection of the largest undeveloped onshore oil prospect in the United States [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The promised benefits — cheaper fuel, energy security, federal and state revenue — are speculative and long-term: the bill itself concedes a ten-or-more-year lead time before major new fields could produce, and new domestic supply would have modest effect on world oil prices set globally. The costs are concrete and permanent: industrial development of the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and other wildlife habitat, on terms set by a review standard frozen at 1987. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill's 'expeditious' leasing mandate and its ban on further study were designed to short-circuit the environmental debate, not resolve it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Murkowski of Alaska introduced the bill on January 14, 1991, joined by five other senators as original introducers, including Senator Ted Stevens of Alaska [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on January 14, 1991 [S5].
Thirteen senators cosponsored the bill, twelve Republicans and one Democrat [S4].
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — was ever recorded before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Arctic coastal plain remained under the protections Congress set in 1980. Conservation interests, subsistence communities, and everyone who valued leaving the refuge undeveloped came out ahead; oil companies gained nothing and lost the lease sale the bill would have required within a year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Conservation interests; oil companies gained nothing

for.name: Frank Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill to open the coastal plain to leasing, as he did repeatedly across his career.

for.name: Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original co-introducer of the bill.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by J. Bennett Johnston (D-LA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: National environmental and conservation organizations
against.what_they_did: Long-standing public opposition to development of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain shaped the politics of any ANWR bill in this era.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The bill's sponsors and 12 of its 13 cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democratic cosponsor, but no committee or floor action ever revealed how the Senate as a whole stood.

industries.note: The bill would have handed companies competitive leases on the coastal plain — the most sought-after undeveloped onshore prospect in the country — with lease terms running as long as oil is produced. The bill directed the Secretary to maximize Treasury revenue while giving independent producers a competitive shot at bids. Its gain is exclusive access to public land whose environmental value would be foregone.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and North Slope communities
industries.note: The bill directs impact aid, planning advice, and public-services assistance to North Slope communities, and all receipts from leases flow to the Treasury under the applicable Alaska allocation law. Local governments and residents affected by development would be compensated.

industries.industry: Trans-Alaska Pipeline System operators and shippers
industries.note: The bill's findings warn that declining Prudhoe Bay production could force pipeline shutdown within ten years and strand reserves. New coastal plain fields would extend the pipeline's life and throughput, mainly benefiting its owners and North Slope producers.
